summary: The whole of the correspondence: Wilde thanking George Bedborough, who had had his essays bound up from the periodicals, ten weeks before Bedborough's arrest for selling Havelock Ellis's book.
certainty_reasoning: The record documents a friendship or acquaintance with no evidence of attraction or romance; classified platonic, upgradable if contrary evidence comes to light.

sources.quote: My dear Sir, I must thank you very much for the books: the edition of my essays is a masterpiece of lovely binding and I was charmed to receive my dear father's book, and also _*Salomé*_ with the dainty drawings of Max Beerbohm in his Oxford days. You really have been most kind to me and I _do_ hope to see you. I am worried over the sordid things of life, so cannot write - at least intelligently - but I beg you to accept again my sincere thanks and I hope you will review '*The Ballad of Reading Gaol*' somewhere. You have been so charming to the author, that you may be charming also to the work. Truly yours
sources.context: Wilde to George Bedborough, [postmark 15 March 1898], Hôtel de Nice, Paris (MS Texas) - quoted whole. Bedborough had had Wilde's essays bound up out of the periodicals they first appeared in and inscribed the volume 'To the author from Geo. Bedborough, 5 March 1898'. Read the dates together: this is 15 March; Bedborough reviewed The Ballad in the April Adult, hoping Wilde's next song would be 'signed with the old familiar name'; and on 31 May he was arrested for selling Havelock Ellis's Sexual Inversion to a plain-clothes policeman. 'My dear father's book' is one of Sir William Wilde's.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The whole of the correspondence, ten weeks before Bedborough's arrest.
sources.provenance: PDF p. 1083. Checked against the manuscript, HRC MSS_WildeO_2_4_029-031, with the envelope at _026-027. Marks reproduced as Wilde made them. Two underlines: 'do' for stress, and the title 'Salome', which carries the underline a hand uses where type would be italic, so it is marked as both. The title of the Ballad carries NO underline - Wilde set it in SINGLE QUOTATION MARKS, restored here; the printed page removes them and prints the title in italic instead, per the editors' standardisation of titles. The italic is kept as this map's own convention for a book title. He wrote the marks across three lines, repeating them at each break - 'The / 'Ballad of Reading' / Gaol' - which is a line-wrap convention rather than four separate quotations; since non-paragraph line breaks are not preserved in these transcriptions, the repeats are normalised to one opening and one closing mark.
